test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 19 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: What is a decomposition reaction?

options.text: A compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances
Two or more substances combine to form one product
A single substance is formed from two or more reactants

solution:
The correct answer is __**A compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Decomposition reaction** is a fundamental type of chemical process where a **single reactant** breaks down into **two or more simpler products**. This is the exact definition provided in the first option. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• In these reactions, the **chemical bonds** in the reactant molecule are broken, requiring an input of energy. The general chemical equation for this process can be represented as **AB → A + B**.
 
• Statement 2 describes a **Double Displacement reaction**, where **two compounds exchange ions** to form two new compounds, often resulting in a precipitate or water. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• Statement 3 and Statement 4 describe a **Combination reaction** (also known as a synthesis reaction), where **two or more substances combine** to form a **single product**. This is the opposite of decomposition. ***Hence, statement 3 and 4 are incorrect.***
 
• A classic example of decomposition is the **thermal decomposition of Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3)**, which, when heated, yields **Calcium Oxide (CaO)** and **Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Decomposition Reactions:**
 
 
• **Thermal Decomposition:** This occurs when **heat energy** is used to break down a substance. For instance, heating **Lead Nitrate** crystals leads to the emission of **brown fumes of Nitrogen Dioxide** and the formation of Lead Oxide.
 
• **Electrolytic Decomposition (Electrolysis):** This process uses **electrical energy** to drive the decomposition. A primary **example** is the **electrolysis of water**, where water (H2O) decomposes into **Hydrogen gas** and **Oxygen gas** when an electric current is passed through it.
 
• **Photolytic Decomposition (Photolysis):** This breakdown is triggered by **light energy (photons)**. For example, **Silver Chloride (AgCl)** turns **grey** in sunlight because it decomposes into **Silver metal** and **Chlorine gas**.
 
 
 
• **Combination Reactions:** 
 
 
• These are reactions where a **single substance** is formed from multiple reactants. A common **example** is the **burning of magnesium ribbon** in air to form **Magnesium Oxide** or the **burning of coal** (Carbon + Oxygen → Carbon Dioxide).
 
 
 
• **Double Displacement Reactions:**
 
 
• These involve the **exchange of ions** between reactants. A well-known **example** is the reaction between **Sodium Sulphate** and **Barium Chloride**, which produces a **white precipitate** of **Barium Sulphate** and Sodium Chloride.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Energy Nature:** Most decomposition reactions are **endothermic** in nature because they involve the **absorption of energy** (heat, light, or electricity) to break existing chemical bonds.
 
• **Biological Application:** Decomposition reactions are vital in the **human body**. During **digestion**, complex food molecules like **starch** and **proteins** undergo decomposition reactions to break down into simpler substances like **glucose** and **amino acids**, which the body can then absorb.
 
• **Industrial Use:** Decomposition of **Calcium Carbonate** is a key step in the **manufacturing of cement**. The **Calcium Oxide (Quick Lime)** produced is a vital raw material in various industries.
 
• **Photography:** The **photolytic decomposition** of **Silver Bromide (AgBr)** was traditionally used in **Black and White Photography** to capture images on film.
</ul
